analysis.one_liner: Strips government officials of the court-made shield protecting them from lawsuits over rights violations.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted only three sponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would eliminate 'qualified immunity' — a doctrine invented by the Supreme Court in 1967 that shields government employees, including police officers, from being held personally liable for violating someone's constitutional rights unless the right was already 'clearly established.' The bill would restore the standard written into the 1871 civil rights statute itself: if an official acting under state law deprived you of a federal right, you could sue and recover, and good faith or legal confusion would be no defense. It was referred to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by police or other state and local officials. Today, most such lawsuits are thrown out before a jury ever hears them, because the victim must point to a past court case with nearly identical facts proving the right was 'clearly established.' Under this bill, a jury could decide whether the official actually violated the person's rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of rights violations by officials

how_it_helps.text: Removes three defenses — good faith, belief the conduct was lawful, and the 'not clearly established' rule — from civil suits under the 1871 civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983).
Applies to lawsuits already pending as well as suits filed after enactment, so people with cases in court at the time would benefit.
States Congress's position that qualified immunity was never in the statute, tracing how the Supreme Court created it in 1967 and expanded it in 1982, and says courts should apply the law as written.

analysis.who_pays: Government officials who violate rights, and in practice the state and local governments that typically pay court judgments on their employees' behalf. Police departments and city budgets would face more lawsuits reaching juries, and some of those suits would end in damages paid by taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments and police budgets

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to suits already pending at enactment, meaning defendants who relied on the old immunity rules would face changed rules mid-case.

The strongest good-faith objection: officers and other officials making fast decisions would face personal liability without the current 'clearly established' safe harbor, which supporters of the doctrine say chills legitimate police work and floods courts with litigation — and because governments usually indemnify their employees, the cost of settlements and judgments would largely fall on local taxpayers rather than the individual officers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims of rights violations, the benefit is substantial: it converts many currently hopeless lawsuits into ones a jury can actually hear, which is also how future misconduct gets deterred. The honest cost is that local governments and their insurers would pay more in judgments and litigation, and officers would lose the shield for split-second decisions. Supporters argue those are precisely the accountability costs the 1871 Congress intended; opponents argue the doctrine exists to let officials do their jobs without second-guessing. The bill would not have changed criminal liability at all — only the ability to sue for damages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and it never advanced from there before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act in the Senate on March 1, 2021.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day; no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
Only two senators cosponsored the bill: one of 48 Senate Democrats and one of two Senate Independents. No Republican signed on.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any other recorded action, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials, including police officers, keep the qualified immunity shield, so lawsuits over constitutional violations can still be dismissed without a trial when the right was not 'clearly established.' People seeking to hold officials accountable in court gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the chamber's position was never tested; on the record, only three progressive Democratic and Independent senators sponsored the bill and no Republican ever signed on.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill would remove the personal-liability shield that currently gets most lawsuits against officers dismissed before trial. Police unions are the most prominent defenders of qualified immunity, though no opposition action appears in this bill's record.

Cities, counties, and their insurers would pay more settlements and judgments because governments typically indemnify employees, but they would also gain from clearer liability rules and from misconduct being deterred and exposed in court.
